name: Rate-Limited API Gateway with Circuit Breaker

nodes.name: API Gateway Fetch Webhook
nodes.notes: POST { integration, resource_path, params?, cache_key, max_staleness_seconds? }. A front door your other workflows call instead of hitting a rate-limited API directly. Rate limiting, circuit breaking and graceful degradation live here, once.

nodes.name: Evaluate Breaker State
nodes.notes: 'open_no_probe' means the breaker is open and its cooldown hasn't elapsed -- skip straight to degrade, don't even ask for a rate-limit token. 'open_due_probe' means it's time to test recovery with exactly one call.

nodes.name: Claim Probe Slot
nodes.notes: Atomic compare-and-set, valid for PROBE_CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS. When the cooldown ends and several queued requests all become eligible, exactly one gets claimed:true and makes the real test call; the rest degrade. The atomicity lives in your state service -- see README.

parameters.jsCode:
const t = $json;
return [{ json: { integration: t.integration, resource_path: t.resource_path, params: t.params, cache_key: t.cache_key, max_staleness_seconds: t.max_staleness_seconds, is_probe: true, attempt: 1 } }];

nodes.name: Consume Rate Limit Token
nodes.notes: One atomic call: check-and-decrement the token bucket in the state service, never a separate check-then-consume pair. Bucket size comes from the provider's rate_limit settings in CONFIG.PROVIDERS_JSON.

nodes.name: Token Available?
nodes.notes: A proactive, self-imposed limit sized to the provider's quota, so you rarely hit the real 429. If the rate-limit service itself is unreachable, RATE_LIMIT_FAIL_OPEN decides: true = let the call through, false = degrade.

parameters.jsCode:
const t = $json;
return [{ json: { integration: t.integration, resource_path: t.resource_path, params: t.params, cache_key: t.cache_key, max_staleness_seconds: t.max_staleness_seconds, is_probe: false, attempt: 1 } }];

nodes.name: Call Provider API
nodes.notes: Provider URL, auth headers and timeout come from CONFIG.PROVIDERS_JSON / PROVIDER_TIMEOUT_MS. onError 'continueErrorOutput' is deliberate and different from neverError: neverError keeps non-2xx HTTP statuses on the normal output; it does nothing for connection-level failures (DNS, refused, timeout), which never produce an HTTP response. Those go to this node's error output and are treated like a 5xx.

nodes.name: Classify Response
nodes.notes: 429 is kept distinct from a generic 5xx on purpose: it means 'you're fine, just slow down,' not 'something is broken.' It's handled with Retry-After-aware backoff and doesn't count toward the circuit breaker's failure threshold the way a real server error does.

nodes.name: Record Breaker Success
nodes.notes: A successful probe fully closes the breaker and resets its failure/trip counters server-side -- a successful call while already closed just resets the failure streak. Fire-and-forget: it doesn't gate the response, since the fetch itself already succeeded.

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ body: JSON.stringify($json.body ?? null), cached_at: Date.now() }) }}

nodes.name: Write Cache (Last-Known-Good)
nodes.notes: Every fresh success refreshes the degrade-path cache -- a cache write failure here costs a little staleness next time something goes wrong, never the current, already-successful response.

nodes.name: Parse Retry-After Header
nodes.notes: Retry-After may be seconds or an HTTP-date; both are handled and the result is capped at RETRY_AFTER_CAP_SECONDS. Keep the cap under ~60s: n8n holds short waits in memory, but longer waits are offloaded and a waiting webhook caller can time out.

nodes.name: Rate-Limit Retry Attempts Left?
nodes.notes: A probe call never retries in place -- a probe is one shot to test recovery; if it gets rate-limited, that's still useful information (the breaker stays open) rather than spending the one probe slot's TTL on retries.

parameters.jsCode:
const t = $json;
return [{ json: { integration: t.integration, resource_path: t.resource_path, params: t.params, cache_key: t.cache_key, max_staleness_seconds: t.max_staleness_seconds, is_probe: t.is_probe, attempt: t.attempt + 1 } }];

const t = $json;
return [{ json: { integration: t.integration, cache_key: t.cache_key, max_staleness_seconds: t.max_staleness_seconds, degrade_reason: 'rate_limited_retries_exhausted', retry_after_seconds: t.retry_after_seconds } }];

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ is_probe: $json.is_probe, error_message: $json.network_error ? 'connection error' : ('HTTP ' + $json.statusCode), failure_threshold: $('CONFIG').first().json.FAILURE_THRESHOLD, cooldown_seconds: $('CONFIG').first().json.COOLDOWN_SECONDS, max_cooldown_seconds: $('CONFIG').first().json.MAX_COOLDOWN_SECONDS }) }}

nodes.name: Record Breaker Failure
nodes.notes: The thresholds travel with the request, so tuning the breaker means editing CONFIG, not the service. A failed probe re-opens the breaker immediately with a longer cooldown (the service doubles it per trip, capped at MAX_COOLDOWN_SECONDS).

nodes.name: Compute Jittered Backoff
nodes.notes: Exponential backoff from BACKOFF_BASE_MS plus random jitter up to BACKOFF_JITTER_MS. Small on purpose: this runs inside a synchronous webhook, so the caller is waiting.

parameters.jsCode:
const t = $json;
return [{ json: { integration: t.integration, resource_path: t.resource_path, params: t.params, cache_key: t.cache_key, max_staleness_seconds: t.max_staleness_seconds, is_probe: t.is_probe, attempt: t.attempt + 1 } }];

nodes.name: Respond (Permanent Error, Passthrough)
nodes.notes: A 4xx that isn't 429 means the request we sent is wrong (bad params, missing auth, not found), not that the provider is unhealthy. Mirroring the status back to the original caller, untouched by retry or breaker logic, is the honest answer -- retrying a malformed request three times with backoff would just be slower wrongness.

nodes.name: Get Cached Response
nodes.notes: A cache miss (or an unreachable cache service) is treated as 'no cached copy', never as an error.

nodes.name: Evaluate Cache Usability
nodes.notes: max_staleness_seconds is caller-controlled on purpose -- a dashboard widget might happily take an hour-old cached value, while a payment-status check might rather fail loudly than show stale data. When the caller doesn't specify it, any cache hit at all is considered usable.

parameters.responseBody: ={{ { data: $json.cached_body, stale: true, served_from: 'cache', age_seconds: $json.age_seconds, degrade_reason: $json.degrade_reason } }}

nodes.name: Respond 200 (Stale, Degraded)
nodes.notes: Graceful degradation's whole payoff: the caller gets a usable answer and an honest 'this is stale and why' instead of an outage propagating straight through to them.

nodes.name: Respond 503 (Unavailable)
nodes.notes: Even the failure response is actionable -- a Retry-After header and an explicit reason (breaker open / rate limited / provider erroring) rather than a bare 503, and cache_available:false tells the caller this integration has literally never succeeded yet, which is a different problem than 'temporarily down'.

nodes.name: CONFIG
nodes.notes: THE ONLY NODE YOU NEED TO EDIT. Every URL, credential header, limit, timeout and threshold lives here. See the sticky note and README for what each value does.

parameters.content:
## Rate-Limited API Gateway with Circuit Breaker
**Setup (about 5 minutes)**
1. Run a state service that implements the HTTP contract in the README (a reference one is included: `node mock-server.js`).
2. Open the **CONFIG** node and set the three service URLs, `STATE_API_HEADERS_JSON` if your service needs auth, and `PROVIDERS_JSON` (one entry per API you front).
3. Activate the workflow and POST to `/webhook/gateway/fetch`.

**Adding another API** = add a key to `PROVIDERS_JSON`. No node changes.

**Tuning** (thresholds, cooldowns, retries, timeouts) = CONFIG only.

Nothing else in this workflow contains a URL, secret or limit.
